title: George (23 April)
hookLine: a soldier-martyr whose dragon is a legend, patron of England and other lands

lines: A RED CROSS, A KNIGHT, A DRAGON.
cards: A red cross on a white field, flying over a stadium in England. A knight on a horse, spearing a dragon, on a gold coin, a church window, a pub sign.
A painted icon in an Orthodox church, the same young rider, the same twisting beast under his hooves. The man in all of them is George. Yet the dragon is the part tradition added later.
Behind the horse and the spear stands a much plainer story: a soldier, and a choice.

teach.h: A SOLDIER WHO WOULD NOT SACRIFICE.
teach.b: Here's what tradition holds about George himself. He was a soldier in the Roman army in the east, a Christian, at a time when an emperor ordered Christians to sacrifice to the gods. George would not.
He was tortured and put to death, and Christians began to honor his grave. Beyond that, the details are thin, and the Church is frank about it.

teach.h: HIS DEEDS KNOWN ONLY TO GOD.
teach.b: An early Church decree, long credited to a pope, counted him among saints whose names people rightly honor but whose deeds are known only to God. Then the dragon.
In a medieval collection of saints' lives called the Golden Legend, a dragon terrorizes a city, demanding victims, until the lot falls on the king's daughter.
George rides up, wounds the beast in the name of Christ, and the princess leads it into the city on her own sash. The people ask for baptism.

It's a legend, and a beloved one, told and painted across Europe and the Christian East. The Church holds both pieces: the martyr, whose feast it keeps, and the legend, free to be what it is, a picture.

Saint Paul gives the same picture without the scales, in the Douay-Rheims: "Put you on the armour of God, that you may be able to stand against the deceits of the devil." The dragon in the story stands for evil.

teach.h: HIS REAL DRAGON WAS AN ORDER.
teach.b: The real George's dragon was an order he would not obey.

teach.h: PUT YOU ON THE ARMOUR OF GOD.
teach.b: England, Georgia, Catalonia and other places took him as patron. The legend gave him a beast. The refusal is the part the oldest tellings already hold.

how: Catholics keep Saint George's optional memorial on 23 April; in England it is a feast, and Orthodox and Eastern Catholic Christians honor him as a great martyr with icons of the rider and the dragon.

games.q: you're George, a Roman soldier and a Christian. the emperor orders every soldier to sacrifice to the gods. what do you do?
games.why: tradition says he refused, and was tortured and put to death. the dragon came later; this was his real fight.

practice: Name one dragon in your own life, not a monster, maybe, but a habit that eats your evenings, a fear you feed to keep it quiet, a demand you keep giving in to.
Look at it plainly, the way George looked at the order he would not obey, and choose one small first move against it.
If you pray, ask for courage, perhaps with the Our Father's line, deliver us from evil; if you don't, just hold your one move steady.

wordCard.voice: George. A soldier martyred for refusing to sacrifice to the gods, whose dragon is a medieval legend, honored as patron of England and other places.

orig.note: Greek: his name as the Christian East writes it.

carryVoice: Your line: slay the dragon. His real fight was a quiet refusal. Day nine hundred eighty-three, done.
